newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich says Congress to quiz Greenspan on growth.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich says Congress to quiz Greenspan on growth.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich, criticising the Federal Reserve for undermining U.S. growth, said on Friday Congress would ask Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan to help raise the annual rate of economic expansion to 4 to 5 percent.

In his first public appearance since returning from a 10-day tour of Asia, the Georgia Republican advocated a heady mix of tax cuts, reform and deregulation as the means for making the U.S. economy emulate the vitality of Taiwan, South Korea and China.

"It is unconscionable to have the Federal Reserve system close off economic growth because of some theoretical model," Gingrich told a business breakfast hosted by his political supporters from his home district.
"Our goal should be to say bluntly, up front: we want a high growth, high income, high take-home pay, high opportunity society," he said. "And we're not going to settle for anything less."

Gingrich told his audience that the Republican-controlled Congress would ask Greenspan to submit a list of fiscal and economic policy changes which, if enacted, would make a 4 to 5 percent growth rate acceptable to a central bank determined to keep inflation in check.

The speaker predicted the Fed chairman, were he speaking in his former role as private-sector economist, would favour a Republican legislative agenda built on the elimination of the capital gains tax and the bulk of regulatory limits on business and industry.

Speaking weeks after he was widely criticised in his own party for suggesting that Congress could make lower taxes a secondary priority, Gingrich called for getting rid of taxes on savings and investments as an incentive to job growth.
He also vowed lawmakers would seek to completely overhaul the Internal Revenue Service if not scrap the federal tax agency altogether.

"You want Chinese or Hong Kong or Taiwanese growth rates? You've got to have a tax system that favours economic growth. If you want more jobs and you want more wealth and you want a better future ... there should be no taxes on savings and investments," he said.

"We believe the Constitution should be amended to require a super-majority to raise taxes, to protect the taxpayer from a political structure that is too willing to use your money to pay off their political cronies," he said.
